British Prime Minister Andy Burnham discussed Argentina’s bid to block a UK-Israeli oil project near the disputed Falkland Islands and its “economic consequences” in a call Friday with US President Donald Trump. The South American nation last week asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) to block the joint hydrocarbon exploration project off Falkland’s coast, in the latest spat over the territory’s sovereignty. Britain and Argentina fought a brief but bitter 10-week war in 1982 over the South Atlantic islands, known to Argentines as Las Malvinas, which failed to change its status as a UK-administered territory. The Falkland Islanders themselves voted overwhelmingly in 2013 to remain British. But Argentina rejects that outcome, arguing that the principle of self-determination does not apply to a population it considers implanted by Britain after 1833. Milei’s administration has notably targeted the Sea Lion oil project — led by Britain’s Rockhopper and Israel’s Navitas — arguing that it violates a UN resolution calling for both sides to desist from unilateral actions until their dispute is resolved. The right-wing leader has also backed a bill that would ban the development of any natural resources in without authorisation from Buenos Aires, raising the penalty set out in an older law. In their call Friday, Burnham and Trump “discussed the Sea Lion project”, Downing Street said in a readout of the conversation. “The prime minister raised the economic consequences of Argentina’s coercive measures for the UK and US and reiterated the importance of respecting the islanders’ right to develop their natural resources.” Burnham’s office did not provide further details about the purported impact of Argentina’s recent move. Its request submitted to ITLOS “seeks to preserve Argentina’s sovereign rights” and “prevent activities authorized unilaterally and illegally by the United Kingdom from exacerbating the dispute recognized by the United Nations,” according to a presidential statement last week.
